source.title: A circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in-context in Large Language Models
source.authors: Tankred Saanum; Can Demircan; Samuel J. Gershman; Eric Schulz

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; no apparent cutoff or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Tests induction-head behavior and its causal contribution to in-context prediction using pretrained LLMs and synthetic hierarchical sequences, rather than reproducing the original training-time method.
record.gate_note: The paper measures adaptive induction-head attention and tests ablations affecting prediction. It does not study induction-head formation during training, training-loss bumps, or the timing of in-context learning gains. Probe decodability values are not included as rows because they concern latent-context representations rather than the claim versions' named behavior. Values available only in figures are recorded as figure only.
record.test_reason: In pretrained 0.5B–3B decoder LLMs, the study ablates induction heads and measures the loss of in-context prediction on hierarchical repetitive sequences (bears on V3). It also identifies induction heads across five model families (bears on V4). It does not use small attention-only models, training dynamics or data manipulations.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially correct. The authors also claim that induction heads, with supporting context-matching heads, offer a unifying account of predicting patterns introduced in-context. They limit this to repetitive and hierarchical structure, and leave abstract (ARC-style) and reasoning-based in-context learning unexplored.
record.recipe_differences: Uses pretrained LLMs on synthetic hierarchical sequences and natural-language prompts, measuring adaptive attention and performing targeted ablations. It does not reproduce the original training-time emergence or loss-curve analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports different behavior for adaptive versus static induction heads and for second- versus third-order sequence criteria; adaptive heads are in later layers while non-adaptive heads appear earlier. It does not state a quantified prompt- or layer-sensitivity sweep.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen2.5-1.5B, ablating previous-token head 13-4 leaves induction head 14-3 attending to successors in general. It removes 14-3's correct-context selection (r17). Separately, ablating context-matching heads cuts both prediction and induction-head accuracy across seven LLMs (r20, r21).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In pretrained LLMs, previous-token-style heads feed latent-context information that lets induction heads select context-appropriate successors. They are not simply the K-composition source for basic induction.

fits_no_version.finding: Later-layer induction heads adapt their attention to context, while earlier-layer static ones do not. On ambiguous natural-language prompts, adaptive head 19-3 prefers the correct successor and static head 2-3 does not (r18, r19).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Some induction heads in LLMs perform context-dependent (higher-order) successor selection rather than plain [A][B]…[A]→[B] copying.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 9th BlackboxNLP Workshop: Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP (listed venue); paper text says preprint, under review.
record.problems: The paper gives many results only in figures without numerical values in the text. The causal tests concern a specific synthetic repetitive-pattern task and a small set of natural-language prompts, so they do not establish the role of induction heads in general few-shot learning. The study does not examine training-time emergence or loss curves.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional attention maps, context-decoding probe results, and per-model figure panels in Figures 3–6 and 9–12. Context-decoding probe results were left out because they measure latent-context representation rather than claim-version behavior; individual numeric figure values are not stated in the text. Aggregate appendix findings are retained in r7–r10 and r21.

untested.parts: All of it: no small attention-only transformers. Composition with a previous-token head is probed only in a pretrained LLM (r17).
All of it: no training dynamics, timing or loss bump.
General in-context learning, per-token loss, few-shot tasks and natural text at scale. Induction-head ablation is only on the synthetic hierarchical task, and only in Qwen2.5.
Other architectures, modalities and multiple training runs.
All of it: no few-shot task-learning comparison.

missing.what: Intact-model accuracy rising with repetitions on 2nd/3rd-order sequences, i.e. in-context learning without ablation. This is the baseline for r11–r13.

record.verdict_notes: Most values are figure-only and no uncertainty is reported. Induction-head ablation (r11–r13) was run only on Qwen2.5; the appendix replications ablate context-matching heads only. The record's V1 links were removed because V1 names small attention-only models. The Figure 2 caption says only some induction heads adapt, and non-induction heads also learn the correct context.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test small attention-only transformers trained from scratch or establish that induction heads form specifically by composing with a previous-token head. It tests adaptive induction behavior and ablations of induction and context-matching heads in pretrained LLMs.
Training-time emergence, abruptness, timing relative to in-context learning gains, and a training-loss bump are not studied.

Does not establish that induction heads explain most in-context learning across large transformers or across general few-shot tasks; its causal tests concern repetitive hierarchical sequence prediction.
Tests selected decoder LLM families and sizes only. It does not test other architectures or modalities, or universality across training runs.
Does not vary training data or training setup, or measure whether in-context learning persists under such changes.
Does not test few-shot task learning or compare its mechanisms with induction heads.
Does not track formation during training or test whether it consists of separate or overlapping transitions.

relation.reason: The study directly measures induction-head behavior across models and tests causal involvement using induction-head and random-head ablations.

tranche.reason: Pretrained-model attention measurements and controlled ablations on hierarchical sequences address induction-head presence and causal involvement through a different experimental method.

source_check.notes: The study measures hierarchical-sequence prediction accuracy, not token-index loss or the share of all in-context learning; abstract and reasoning-based learning remain untested. Exact curve values are unavailable in the supplied text, but the qualitative outcomes are explicit.

statements.correction: Section 3.1: all-induction-head zero-ablation yields chance-level prediction at 0.5B and 1.5B; severely reduced but above-chance prediction at 3B; small or negligible reductions under matched random-head ablation. No normalized induction-head share is reported.
statements.problem: The ablation outcomes are correct, but they do not establish that the induction-head share shrinks with scale or that V3 requires qualification at 3B. Above-chance residual performance is compatible with induction heads carrying most of the effect.
